strengths: Novel contribution: Per-instance noise scheduling guided by image power spectrum is creative and well-motivated
Solid theoretical foundation: Clear analysis connecting spectral properties to noise levels with formal bounds on efficacy
Comprehensive experimental design: Evaluation across multiple resolutions and model sizes with good ablations
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations and clearly specified algorithms
Practical improvements in low-step regime: Demonstrates benefits for fast generation scenarios
Proper mathematical treatment: Variance-preserving assumptions and closed-form schedule solutions provided
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements: Typically <1 FID gain over SiD2; gains disappear at higher step counts
Severely limited evaluation scope: Only ImageNet evaluated; no other domains or tasks assessed
Not applicable to latent diffusion: Restricts to pixel-space single-stage diffusion, increasingly obsolete compared to dominant latent approaches
Computational overhead unaddressed: RAPSD computation per training image cost not quantified or discussed
Hyperparameter sensitivity: Table 5 shows >10% FID variation with different κ values; selection appears ad-hoc
Reproducibility concerns: RAPSD sampling details vague, hyperparameter selection unclear, no code availability mentioned
Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is spectrum fitting and noise scaling; standard components throughout
Loose theoretical bounds: Analysis in Section 4.2 proves existence but lacks practical insight
Power-law assumption robustness unclear: Empirical assumption (Eq. 8) and violation consequences not discussed
Incomplete explanation: Doesn't explain why improvements vanish at higher step counts or when method is preferred

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: adapting noise schedules to per-instance image spectral properties is intuitive and grounded in natural image statistics
Theoretical framework connecting power spectrum analysis (RAPSD) to noise level bounds provides mathematical grounding for the approach
Comprehensive implementation details in appendices including closed-form derivations and hyperparameter specifications support reproducibility
Evaluation across multiple resolutions (128-512) shows effort toward generalization
Well-structured presentation of the main concept with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1)
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements: FID gains of only ~0.26 at best (1.68→1.42 at 256×256) with improvements disappearing at higher NFE, limiting practical significance

Severely limited baseline comparisons: only SiD2 is compared despite multiple recent noise schedule methods being available (Chen et al., Hang et al., Sashoo et al.). No comparison to state-of-the-art or latent diffusion models
Narrow experimental scope: restricted to ImageNet class-conditional generation at three resolutions; no evaluation on unconditional generation, text-to-image, inpainting, or other applications

Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution—computing RAPSD and interpolating predefined schedules—is relatively straightforward, reading more as an engineering refinement than a methodological advance
Incomplete theoretical insights: the theoretical analysis (Section 4.2) primarily applies power spectrum assumptions to derive bounds without providing novel understanding of diffusion dynamics

Confusing presentation of key technical details: unclear methodology for RAPSD computation during training (why ancestral sampling?), poorly explained 'flop heavy' variants, abrupt introduction of mixed schedules and conditioning mechanisms
Missing critical ablations: no systematic study of design choices (frequency-focused vs power-focused), spectrum approximation methods, or hyperparameter sensitivity beyond limited Table 3
No computational cost analysis: per-instance schedule computation overhead not quantified
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite variation across seeds
Generated samples show no visually apparent improvements despite claimed FID gains, raising questions about practical perceptual benefits

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach using image spectral properties to guide per-instance noise schedules, with elegant theoretical justification through rigorous RAPSD analysis

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three resolutions (128², 256², 512²) with multiple metrics, showing consistent improvements especially in the practically-important low-step regime (32-64 steps: 5-15% FID improvements)
Thorough ablation studies systematically validating design choices including schedule variants, FiLM conditioning, and guidance intervals, strengthening the contribution
Solid mathematical framework with clear derivations from spectral properties to noise level bounds and closed-form schedules, with proper variance-preserving assumptions
Excellent presentation and clarity with effective visualizations (Figures 1-3) that clearly convey the method's concept and benefits; detailed implementation details enable reproducibility
Significant practical value: achieving better generation quality with fewer denoising steps directly addresses key efficiency concerns in diffusion model deployment
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: while the application is clever, the core insight that different frequencies warrant different noise treatment follows fairly naturally from natural image statistics
Improvements diminish substantially at higher step counts: at optimal NFE (256 steps for 256²), FID improvement is modest (~7%), limiting applicability for high-quality generation scenarios

Experimental scope is limited to ImageNet class-conditional generation only; lacks evaluation on other datasets, domains, unconditional generation, and text-to-image applications where diffusion models are widely deployed
Theoretical justification relies partially on empirical observations: the maximum noise derivation uses the heuristic condition Ψ_zₑ(q) ≫ 1 without rigorous formal justification of its validity
Computational overhead not quantified: DFT computation for each training image during RAPSD estimation is not measured or discussed; potential impact on training time unclear
Method introduces hyperparameters (κ_min, κ_max, κ_p) requiring resolution-specific tuning (Table 5), reducing generality; systematic sensitivity analysis could be more thorough
Missing important ablations: no direct comparison between per-instance adaptation vs. simpler baseline using fixed global schedule derived from training set median RAPSD
Incomplete failure mode analysis: no discussion of performance on images with atypical spectral properties, synthetic/out-of-distribution images, or other potential edge cases

strengths: Novel per-instance noise scheduling idea grounded in image spectral properties, with clear intuitive motivation (Figure 1)
Solid mathematical framework deriving expected RAPSD after noise addition and bounds on effective noise levels
Comprehensive experiments across multiple resolutions and datasets with fair comparisons against SiD2 baseline
Practical advantages including 3× speedup at optimal steps and no per-resolution hyperparameter tuning
Thorough ablation studies isolating individual contributions and investigating FID degradation at high NFE
Well-executed presentation with clear algorithms, good visualizations, and complete implementation details
weaknesses: Theoretical bounds (κ_min, κ_max) lack rigorous justification; choice of κ_max=100, κ_min=0.01 appears ad-hoc
Mixed schedule design (λ_M = 0.5(λ_F + λ_P)) acknowledged as heuristic, contradicting 'principled' framing; no justification for averaging weights
Power law approximation Ψ̃(k)=βk^α uses only 2 parameters without validating approximation error or sensitivity analysis
Modest empirical improvements in standard regimes (FID gains of 0.05-0.26) with most benefits concentrated in low-step regime
FID degradation at high NFE suggests tight schedules have fundamental limitations; degradation appears earlier than baseline, requiring γ=0.5 adjustment
Poor generalization across domains: text-to-image oracle (6.55 FID) significantly outperforms sampler (7.18 FID), indicating RAPSD sampler doesn't generalize
Significant architectural modifications beyond noise scheduling (min/max logSNR conditioning, t-based guidance intervals) make it difficult to isolate the pure contribution
Results lag substantially behind SOTA (LDMs reach 1.13 FID; method reaches 1.32-1.45), limiting practical impact in field dominated by latent diffusion
Hyperparameter choices (C=5/10 for GMM components, κ values) lack principled justification or sensitivity analysis
Scope limited to single-stage pixel diffusion, which is increasingly sidelined by LDMs and distilled models

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Figure 1 effectively illustrates inefficiency of standard schedules for spectrally different images
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple resolutions, datasets (ImageNet + MS-COCO), metrics (FID, sFID, IS, Precision, Recall), and thorough ablations with fair SiD2 baseline comparison
Honest investigation of limitations: Section C.1 thoroughly analyzes FID degradation at high steps rather than obscuring it
Practical benefits: ~50% reduction in denoising steps at comparable optimal step count provides real computational savings
Technically sound methodology: RAPSD derivations are mathematically correct and the schedule design follows logically from the theoretical bounds
Well-documented implementation: Detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, and ablation studies support reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical: FID degradation at high step counts (Figure 3) contradicts the core premise. Models perform worse than baselines with 512+ steps, suggesting the method trades off one regime for another rather than uniformly improving—this fundamentally undermines the 'tight schedule' concept

Limited novelty: Per-instance spectral adaptation is an incremental extension of existing spectral analysis work (Rissanen 2023, Dieleman 2024, Benita et al. 2025). The step from dataset-level to per-instance trends is natural but not conceptually deep

Marginal quality improvements: ~7% FID reduction in optimal regime (1.68→1.42), and 0% on ImageNet 512×512 FLOP-heavy (1.45→1.45), with gains primarily from step reduction rather than inherent quality improvement

Poor generalization to new domains: Table 3 shows oracle spectrum achieves 6.55 FID vs. learned sampler at 7.08 FID for text-to-image (0.5 FID gap), indicating the RAPSD sampler fails to generalize from ImageNet to COCO, creating a critical bottleneck for zero-shot transfer

Narrow applicability: Only demonstrated on SiD2; no experiments with other recent single-stage methods (PixelDiT, PixelFlow) cited in the paper. Doesn't apply to dominant LDM approaches. Results acknowledged to lag behind state-of-the-art LDMs/distilled models

Ad-hoc design choices: (1) Mixed schedule simply averages two variants without justification; (2) Frequency/power-only variants catastrophically fail (5.16/5.18 FID), suggesting lack of principled design; (3) Guidance interval switch from logSNR to t appears to be a band-aid fix rather than principled modification

Weak theoretical justification: Section 4.2 derives κ_min, κ_max heuristically but doesn't prove optimality for generation quality. The connection between theoretical bounds (Section 4.2) and actual schedule design (Section 4.3) is loose—three different heuristic interpolation schemes undermine claimed principled approach
Incomplete hyperparameter analysis: Despite claims of automatic adaptation, Table 8 shows κ_min, κ_max, and guidance intervals require per-resolution tuning. No principled guidance for new datasets

Missing key comparisons: No experimental comparison with Benita et al. (2025), which also optimizes noise schedules using spectral analysis. Fixed median schedule (Table 2) achieves 1.61 FID vs. 1.42 per-instance, suggesting simple alternatives are surprisingly competitive
Lack of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or analysis despite multiple runs. Improvements reported as point estimates only

strengths: Clear motivation with compelling visual demonstration (Fig. 1) of the core problem that standard schedules apply inappropriate noise to different spectral types
Theoretically grounded approach with sound derivation of minimum/maximum noise level bounds based on spectral properties (Eqs. 9-16)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple resolutions and datasets with fair comparisons using identical architecture to baseline
Strong practical improvements in the computationally important low-step regime (32-256 steps) with 3x speedup at optimal configurations
Extensive ablations and supplementary analysis (Section C) thoroughly investigating design choices and edge cases like high-NFE degradation
Well-documented implementation details, hyperparameters, and algorithms enabling reproducibility
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and generally well-structured writing
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward extension of per-resolution scheduling (SiD2) to per-instance scheduling; three schedule variants are simple heuristics (linear interpolation, CDF-based, simple averaging)
FID degradation at high NFE (Figures 3, Table 4) suggests 'tight' schedules are overly restrictive; mitigation via γ=0.5 undermines the core principle
RAPSD sampler bottleneck: significant oracle gap for zero-shot text-to-image (6.55 vs 7.18 FID at 96 NFE), indicating poor generalization to distribution shifts; limited analysis of failure modes
Incomplete attribution of improvements: Table 2 shows minmax conditioning alone accounts for ~0.16 FID difference, confounding the noise schedule contribution with architectural changes
Theoretical justification incomplete: connection between maintaining tight RAPSD bounds and training efficacy is assumed not empirically validated; no comparison with alternative spectral objectives

Hyperparameter tuning not fully avoided: κ_min and κ_max still require global tuning (Table 6 shows sensitivity); guidance intervals still need per-resolution adjustment; choices framed as 'principled' appear heuristic
Limited scope: improvements modest for compute-heavy models; restricted to pixel diffusion which lags state-of-the-art LDMs; no comparison with other adaptive scheduling methods

Power law assumption (Eq. 8) may not hold universally; fitting quality and failure rates not analyzed; mixed schedule averaging (Eq. 23) acknowledged as heuristic without justification or alternatives explored
Design choice justification weak: why average frequency- and power-focused schedules rather than weighted combination or other blending strategies?
No analysis of RAPSD sampler generalization across datasets or investigation of applicability to latent diffusion models
